title: How A Back-To-School Promise Can Transform Your Teaching Career m-your-teaching-career/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes a ritual he calls the "two-part promise," delivered to a new class after the classroom management plan has been fully taught, modeled, and role-played. The teacher pauses in silence, then solemnly promises to follow the plan exactly and every time misbehavior occurs, followed by a second promise never to yell, scold, use sarcasm, or disrespect students. He instructs teachers to deliver each part slowly, let it linger in silence for thirty seconds, and repeat it for emphasis, arguing the ritual marks a seismic shift in how students perceive the teacher and the classroom. Because it removes both inconsistency and intimidation, the promise is meant to establish leadership and trust so firmly that few students will ever test the teacher again. Linsin frames the act as risky and exhilarating precisely because the teacher's reputation and word are on the line.
points: The strategy is a scripted "two-part promise" delivered after the full classroom management plan has been taught and modeled.
Part one promises to follow the plan exactly, every time; part two promises never to yell, scold, or disrespect students.
Deliver each part slowly with long pauses (30+ seconds) so the words visibly sink in.
Removing both inconsistency and intimidation from the classroom is what makes students stop testing the teacher.
quotes: This week’s strategy, which consists of making a simple, two-part promise to your students, is about throwing your hat over the wall.
I promise to follow the classroom management plan exactly as we’ve learned it and every time someone misbehaves.
Furthermore, I promise to never yell, scold, use sarcasm, or in any way treat you with disrespect.
From this moment on, I will follow our classroom management plan to a tee and never, ever treat you with disrespect.
Said with conviction, the moment will mark a seismic shift in how your students view school and their relationship with their new teacher.
With those two remarkably unsettling possibilities thrown out the window—that is, inconsistency and intimidation—the freedom to learn and truly love school is all that remains.
But if you do it, if you’re willing to bet on yourself and your ability to keep your word, your teaching life will never be the same again.
